beginner.headline: Countries Cannot Agree at Climate Talks
beginner.brief: Nearly 200 countries are trying to agree on a new world climate plan. The talks are in Turkey, but the countries have not agreed on a plan. Teams stopped talking for the night after the meeting ran more than a day late. Some countries want a promise to use less fossil fuel, such as oil, gas and coal. However, the latest plan says nothing about using less fossil fuel. African countries also want promises of more money to prepare for climate problems. Some teams are changing their flights from Sunday to Monday while they wait for a deal. All countries must agree before they can make a deal. The talks could stop if the countries cannot agree. If the talks end without a deal, the countries will meet again next year.

intermediate.headline: Fossil Fuel Dispute Blocks COP31 Climate Agreement
intermediate.brief: Negotiations, or formal discussions, at the COP31 climate meeting in Turkey continued more than a day beyond the planned finish. Countries had still not agreed on a global climate agreement, so the discussions were suspended, or stopped temporarily, for the night. The EU and Pacific island nations opposed a draft agreement, an unfinished version, because it did not mention reducing fossil fuel demand. Ministers from several countries and the EU wanted the final agreement to include a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal. Fossil fuel producers, led by Saudi Arabia, had pushed to remove that commitment from the agreement. The Africa Group wanted commitments, or firm promises, to provide more money for adaptation, which means preparing for climate change's effects. The EU had previously said it would not support this request for more adaptation money. An earlier draft included a target of $120 billion for adaptation by 2035, but this amount was later removed. Some teams were moving their Sunday flights to Monday, suggesting that an agreement was still some distance away. If countries do not reach consensus, meaning agreement among all participants, the negotiations could be suspended. In that case, the meeting would end without an agreement and continue next year. However, the UK's chief negotiator remained hopeful and said her team was still trying to reach an agreement. Another risk was that too many teams might leave, leaving too few countries to approve a global agreement.

advanced.headline: Fossil Fuel Dispute Leaves COP31 in Deadlock
advanced.brief: Negotiations at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey remained in deadlock, with countries unable to agree even after discussions had overrun by more than a day. The EU and Pacific island nations opposed the latest text because it omitted any reference to reducing global demand for fossil fuels. A second sticking point concerned the African Group's request for stronger financial support for adaptation to climate impacts, which the EU had previously opposed. Delegations moving their return flights from Sunday to Monday provided a further indication that agreement remained elusive. Should countries fail to reach the required consensus, the negotiations could be suspended. The summit could then end without agreement and be reconvened next year, an outcome with only one precedent since these climate meetings began in 1995. Ministers sought to have a commitment to shift away from oil, gas and coal reinstated after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal. References to carbon capture, use and storage, a technology that stores released emissions underground, were criticised as a licence to continue burning oil and gas. The proposed agreement could, for the first time at such a summit, acknowledge that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed. Australia's climate change and energy minister, Chris Bowen, resisted calls to include language on fossil fuels. He argued that the summit should prioritise implementation, meaning putting measures into practice, and focus on the transition towards clean energy. Meanwhile, renewable energy was expanding at unprecedented rates, with solar panels making the largest contribution to meeting new global energy demand that year and outstripping oil and gas. One reported proposal would keep fossil fuels off the table in exchange for Saudi Arabia and other fossil fuel producers pledging to obtain 35% of their energy consumption from electricity by 2035. An earlier objective of increasing adaptation funding to $120 billion by 2035 had been removed from the text. Ghana's environment minister presented funding as a rightful claim on behalf of people bearing the brunt of developed countries' activities. The departure of negotiating teams could also leave too few nations present to pass a global agreement.
